Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is a well-established treatment modality for a variety of malignant diseases as well as for inborn errors of the metabolism or immune system. Regardless of disease origin, good clinical effects are dependent on proper immune reconstitution. T cells are responsible for both the beneficial graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) effect against malignant cells and protection against infections. The immune recovery of T cells relies initially on peripheral expansion of mature cells from the graft and later on the differentiation and maturation from donor-derived hematopoietic stem cells. The formation of new T cells occurs in the thymus and as a byproduct, T cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) are released upon rearrangement of the T cell receptor. Detection of TRECs by PCR is a reliable method for estimating the amount of newly formed T cells in the circulation and, indirectly, for estimating thymic function. Here, we discuss the role of TREC analysis in the prediction of clinical outcome after allogeneic HSCT. Due to the pivotal role of T cell reconstitution we propose that TREC analysis should be included as a key indicator in the post-HSCT follow-up. TREC transplantation immune reconstitution 1. Allogeneic Stem Cell Transplantation Over the past five decades, progress within the field of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) has been astonishing, making it one of current medicine’s fastest expanding disciplines. Advances have markedly reduced risks, improved outcome, and widened the indications for the procedure. HSCT is currently a valid second or third line option for life-threatening conditions when no alternative treatments are available. The difficulty in foreseeing certain complications post-HSCT, such as relapse and infectious complications, is one of the main problems. 1.1. Indications for Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT) Initially, HSCT was restricted to patients with acute leukemia, severe aplastic anemia (SAA), or severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) [ 1 , 2 ]. Over the years indications for treatment have widened to chronic leukemias, lymphomas, multiple myeloma, myelodysplastic syndromes, and diverse forms of inherited metabolic, hematologic and immunologic disorders. Additionally, HSCT has been evaluated—with encouraging results—as a treatment for other diseases not conventionally considered for transplant, for instance renal cell carcinoma, sickle cell anemia, beta thalassemia major, and some autoimmune disorders [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ]. Clinical HSCT is a quickly changing field with new methods, guidelines and treatment modalities frequently presented into routine practice. The European group for Blood and Marrow Transplantation (EBMT) and its American equivalent, Center for International Blood and Marrow Transplant Research (CIBMTR), frequently update guidelines and recommendations regarding the current practice of and indications for HSCT [ 8 , 9 ]. 1.2. Conditioning Therapy A preparative treatment (conditioning) starts the HSCT procedure. It aims to prevent graft rejection and, in malignancies, to reduce the relapse risk. Initially, total body irradiation (TBI) and high dose cyclophosphamide (Cy) were used as separate conditioning regimens and were later combined for better effect [ 10 , 11 ]. Results were promising; more than half of the initial patients remained disease-free five years after transplant [ 12 ]. Introducing the alkylating agent busulfan (Bu) in later transplants offered an alternative to the logistically more demanding TBI-based regimens [ 13 , 14 ]. As early as the 1950s it was discovered that HSCT provided an additional anti-leukemic effect to that delivered by the myeloablative conditioning alone [ 15 , 16 ]. It eventually became clear that sustained disease remission after HSCT was highly dependent on a continued reaction between the allogeneic immune system and the malignant recipient cells [ 17 , 18 , 19 ]. Based on these findings, new conditioning regimens were developed [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ]. These new non-myeloablative or reduced-intensity conditioning (RIC) regimens were associated with a significant reduction of transplant-related mortality (TRM). This development also made HSCT available for new cohorts of patients for whom the treatment had previously not been considered a safe option, i.e. older patients or those with co-morbidity. Conditioning regimens are, in some instances, combined with the use of inhibiting monoclonal or polyclonal antibodies against T cells [ 24 ]. The main effect of the anti-T cell serotherapy is to prevent rejection by a reducing patient T cell numbers. However, anti-T cell serotherapy may also reduce the risk for graft-versus-host-disease (GVHD) through a delayed suppressive effect on donor T cells. 1.3. Infectious Complications The first months post-HSCT are characterized by profound immunodeficiency, in which the patients are at risk of opportunistic infections. Susceptibility to microbial pathogens decreases gradually as the immune system regains its functionality. Different periods can be distinguished based on the incidence of specific infections after HSCT. The predominance of certain pathogens in each period is a reflection of the type of cell subset deficiency post-HSCT. Not only immune reconstitution is linked to the occurrence of infections post-HSCT. There is also an association between acute GVHD and an increased predisposition to infections. This is thought to be a consequence of the immune modulatory effect of the ongoing systemic inflammation. However, the disturbance of epithelial barriers during conditioning is also a contributing factor [ 25 , 26 ]. In addition, the immunosuppressive drugs used to treat GVHD impair the immune system’s ability to combat infections. 1.4. T Cells—The Double Edged Sword GVHD, i.e., an unwanted immunologic reaction of donor lymphocytes against patient tissue, remains one of the major obstacles post-HSCT, as it causes significant morbidity and mortality. GVHD is seen in both an acute and chronic form, with individual symptoms and diverse pathophysiological mechanisms, which are not all well understood [ 27 ]. Most patients undergoing HSCT receive continuous immunosuppressive treatment during the first 3–6 months post-HSCT to prevent an allogeneic response against healthy tissue. Methotrexate (MTX) and/or cyclosporine A (CsA) is mostly used. All currently available GVHD prophylaxis options inhibit T cell reactivity [ 28 , 29 , 30 ]. Donor T cells can be inactivated for a long period through administration of neutralizing anti-T cell antibodies, either ex vivo or in vivo. These approaches are collectively termed T cell depletion. While they have the potential to eliminate the risk for GVHD, there is also a significantly increased risk of relapse. In parallel with the development of more effective immunosuppressive protocols, advances in human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-typing have significantly contributed to reducing the incidence and severity of GVHD, increasing the rates of engraftment and improving overall survival (OS) [ 31 , 32 , 33 ]. The fundamental treatment option for acute GVHD is still systemic administration of corticosteroids in addition to standard immunosuppression protocols. The effectiveness of HSCT against malignant disorders is dependent on the immunological response between donor-derived lymphocytes and neoplastic cells. This is referred to as the graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) or graft-versus-tumor (GVT) reaction, and explains why HSCT, despite the risk of severe complications, still offers a survival advantage for patients with late-stage malignant disorders when compared to other treatments. Several observations have led to the general recognition of the importance of this phenomenon. In the clinical setting, it was noted that patients who developed GVHD after HSCT had a significantly lower risk of relapse than those who did not show any symptoms of GVHD [ 18 , 19 , 34 ]. Analogously, it was shown that discontinuation of immunosuppression, with the resulting occurrence of GVHD, could be used to re-establish remission in the case of relapsed leukemia after HSCT [ 35 , 36 , 37 ]. The vital role of allo-reactive T cells in GVT reaction and GVHD is illustrated by the fact that both processes are virtually absent in transplantations with grafts fully depleted of T cells [ 38 ]. In addition, they seem to depend strongly upon some degree of histo-incompatibility between donor and recipient. There is also data suggesting that NK cells may contribute to the GVT reaction. This seems to be more pronounced against malignant cells of the myeloid lineage through inhibitory and activating NK cell receptors [ 39 , 40 , 41 ]. The GVT effect is in many cases associated with ongoing GVHD, presumably because of common elements in the mechanism of action [ 18 , 19 , 38 , 42 ]. However, this seems only to be the case if the GVH reaction is initiated against host-specific antigens expressed by malignant cells as well as healthy host cells [ 43 , 44 , 45 ]. It is also reasonable to conclude that these antigens often consist of minor histocompatibility antigens (MiHA) rather than HLA, as the GVT effect is present in transplantations with HLA-identical siblings and there does not seem to be a significant difference in the relapse rate between HSCT with HLA mismatched (MM) and fully matched donors [ 46 ]. Moreover, some antigens are only expressed on tumor cells. These tumor-specific or tumor-associated antigens do not seem to be able to autonomously elicit an allogeneic reaction but may contribute to the GVL effect once an immune response against MiHA has been established [ 47 , 48 , 49 , 50 , 51 ]. Many investigators believe that the GVT effect may be separated from GVHD and this is currently the subject of active research.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Post-allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) for immune reconstitution, complications, and clinical outcome, including T cell recovery, infection risk (opportunistic, bacterial, CMV), relapse, transplant-related mortality (TRM), and Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD). Also in HIV infection, rheumatoid arthritis (RA), multiple sclerosis (MS), and in studies comparing CD31+ vs CD31- na	ifve CD4+ T cells and PTK7+ vs PTK7- na	ifve T cells. Influenced by recipient age, conditioning regimen (RIC vs MAC), stem cell dose, stem cell source (PBSC vs BM), and chimerism status; also in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). Pre-transplantation values are also assessed for predictive value for infections and survival.
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: Serves as a predictive marker. Higher levels are associated with better clinical outcome, improved overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), decreased incidence of severe GVHD, lower incidence of opportunistic/bacterial/CMV infections, and reduced risk of death/relapse post-HSCT. Low levels are significantly correlated with severe opportunistic infections, increased incidence of severe bacterial and CMV infection, increased TRM, and relapse. TREC levels are decreased in HIV-infected patients, RA, and MS, but rapidly increase after HIV treatment. No reduction observed in JIA. CD31+ thymic na	ifve CD4+ T cells and PTK7+ na	ifve T cells contain higher sjTREC/TREC levels. TREC levels are negatively correlated with recipient age (before and after transplant) but positively correlated with the onset of thymic activity after HSCT. Conditioning regimens (RIC) show conflicting results, with some studies reporting significantly higher or rapid increases, while others find no significant differences or negative correlations. Stem cell doses (>10^7 CD34+ PBSC per kg) show significantly higher TREC levels in some studies, suggesting a threshold effect. BM grafts show higher TREC levels compared to PBSC. Impacted by chronic GVHD (absent levels found) and associated with delayed thymic function with acute GVHD. Absent levels in mixed chimerism leading to relapse, but faster immune reconstitution with prolonged mixed chimerism in pediatric patients.
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Detected by PCR to reliably estimate newly formed T cells and thymic function, acting as a quantitative, precise, and noninvasive biomarker for thymic output. Quantification methods vary (absolute, relative by delta-CT, per cell, per mL, or per 	µg of DNA), leading to significant variation in published results. Decreased in HIV-infected patients compared to age-matched healthy controls, with a rapid increase after treatment. Marked reduction in 51 RA patients compared to 47 healthy controls, but no reduction in 70 JIA children vs 110 healthy controls. Decreased significantly in MS. CD31+ thymic na	ifve CD4+ T cell subsets contain higher sjTREC than CD31- central na	ifve CD4+ T cell subsets. PTK7+ na	ifve T cells contain higher levels of TRECs. Low/almost immeasurable levels are significantly correlated with severe opportunistic infections. Lower pre-transplant values are significantly associated with increased incidence of severe bacterial and CMV infection, while high values correlate with better survival. Effective TREC recovery at 6, 9, and 12 months post-HSCT is associated with a 3-, 4-, and 9-fold lower risk of developing severe infections, respectively. Lower sjTREC levels are significantly lower in patients who relapsed. Strong correlation with reduced TRM. CMV clearance efficiency is higher in patients with TREC levels above 2000 copy/	µg DNA. Improved OS and PFS are significantly associated with higher TREC levels. Patients remaining TREC negative for more than a year post-non-myeloablative HSCT developed acute GVHD grade II and III.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT); T cell reconstitution via thymic-dependent pathway; Thymic output and T cell reconstitution; Identification of Recent Thymic Emigrants (RTE); Disease pathophysiology in autoimmune disorders and immunodeficiencies; GVHD prediction; Clinical factors compromising the thymus post-HSCT.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: T cells are crucial for beneficial graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) effect and protection against infections post-HSCT. T cell immune recovery involves peripheral expansion and later differentiation/maturation from donor-derived hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). New T cell formation in the thymus releases T cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) as a byproduct during T cell receptor rearrangement. TRECs are stable, non-replicating extrachromosomal DNA circles that dilute with cell division, serving as a marker for de novo generation of na	ifve T cells differentiated in the recipient thymus. The 	δRec-	ΨJ	α signal joint TREC (sjTREC) is considered the optimal target for measurement due to its late deletion and less dilution. The diversity of the T cell receptor repertoire depends on thymic export of new na	ifve T cells. CD31+thymic na	ifve CD4+ T cells, characterized by higher sjTREC, broader TCR repertoire, higher telomere length, and telomerase activity, are suitable candidates for assessing thymic output due to lower replicative history. PTK7+ na	ifve T cells also contain higher TRECs and produce less IL-2 and IFN gamma, suggesting they identify RTE. Impaired thymic function, indicated by reduced TREC levels, is implicated in autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis. TREC levels correlate with na	ifve T cell numbers post-transplant, predicting T cell reconstitution. TREC is proposed to reflect the thymic ability to produce na	ifve, less alloreactive recipient T cells, thereby predicting GVHD risk. The rate and final degree of T cell reconstitution is a complex interaction influenced by thymic function, GVHD, immunosuppression, conditioning regimen, and viral pathogens. Aging disrupts the thymic microenvironment and affects essential cytokine levels. Pre-transplant radiation dose (conditioning regimen) affects thymic regenerative capacity, may reduce IL-7 production, and total body irradiation (TBI) compromises cortical and medullary thymic epithelial cells (TEC). GVHD induces thymic damage via direct attack of allogeneic immune cells and potentially through immunosuppressive drugs (corticosteroids, cyclosporine). The beneficial role of mesenchymal stem cells and dendritic cells in BM grafts may explain higher TREC levels.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Reduced-intensity conditioning (RIC) regimens (non-myeloablative) led to a significant reduction of transplant-related mortality (TRM) compared to earlier regimens (total body irradiation (TBI) and high dose cyclophosphamide, or busulfan). Conflicting findings exist regarding TREC levels with RIC versus Myeloablative Conditioning (MAC); some studies show significantly higher TREC levels or rapid increases with RIC, while others found no significant differences or even a negative correlation. Variability in TREC quantification methods (absolute vs. relative, different units like TREC per cell, per mL, or per 	µg DNA) leads to significant variation in published results. For stem cell dose, Eyrich et al. reported significantly higher TREC levels with doses >10^7 CD34+ peripheral blood stem cells per kg, but suggested a threshold effect rather than a linear association; other studies found no significant correlation. TREC values are significantly higher in Cord Blood Transplantation (CBT) patients compared to Bone Marrow Transplantation (BMT) patients, attributed to the very na	ifve characteristics of umbilical cord blood. Patients with normal pre-transplant TREC levels show higher post-transplant TREC and T cell counts. Effective TREC recovery at 6, 9, and 12 months post-HSCT is associated with a 3-, 4-, and 9-fold lower risk of severe infections, respectively, indicating a time-dependent protective effect. CMV clearance efficiency is higher in patients with TREC levels above 2000 copy/	µg DNA, and improved OS/PFS is associated with higher TREC levels, suggesting a threshold effect. Persistent TREC negativity (>1 year) post-non-myeloablative HSCT is linked to acute GVHD grade II and III. The effect of immunosuppressive drugs on thymocytes was revealed in vitro and in mice models.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: TRECs are stable DNA circles that do not replicate during mitosis, diluting with each division. The 	δRec-	ΨJ	α signal joint TREC (sjTREC) is considered the optimal target for measurement due to its specificity to late rearrangements and less dilution. The SYBR-Green dye method for detection is less specific compared to TaqMan site-specific probes. SjTREC levels are influenced by longevity of na	ifve T cells, peripheral expansion, apoptosis, and intracellular degradation, requiring careful interpretation. The graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) reaction depends on continued interaction between the allogeneic immune system and malignant recipient cells. GVL and graft-versus-host-disease (GVHD) are virtually absent in T cell-depleted grafts and depend strongly on some degree of histo-incompatibility. NK cells contribute to the GVT reaction, particularly against myeloid lineage malignant cells. TREC levels serve as a surrogate marker specifically for thymic output and are indicative of functional T cell immunity reconstitution post-HSCT, with high predictive value for outcomes like severe infections and survival rates. TREC used for SCID screening showed 100% specificity when combined with IL7, and 100% sensitivity for TREC alone. Lower pre-transplant TREC values are significantly associated with increased severe bacterial and CMV infection incidence, while high TREC values correlate with better survival. Low TREC levels are correlated with severe opportunistic infections, predicting morbidity and mortality after HSCT. Lower sjTREC levels predict relapse in children with hematological malignancies and AML patients, and survival in chronic leukemia. A limitation of CD31 as an RTE marker is noted: not all CD31+ cells are necessarily RTE.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Patients undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) for malignant diseases (e.g., acute/chronic leukemias, lymphomas, multiple myeloma, myelodysplastic syndromes), inborn errors of metabolism or immune system (e.g., severe aplastic anemia (SAA), severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), inherited metabolic/hematologic/immunologic disorders), and other conditions (e.g., renal cell carcinoma, sickle cell anemia, beta thalassemia major, some autoimmune disorders). This includes older patients or those with co-morbidity who receive reduced-intensity conditioning. Also, infants with Congenital SCID; Patients with immunodeficiency disorders (CD4+ T lymphocytopenia, 22q11.2 deletion syndromes); HIV-infected patients; Patients with autoimmune diseases (Rheumatoid arthritis, Multiple Sclerosis, Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis); HSCT recipients, including pediatric recipients, those with malignant hematological diseases, AML patients, chronic leukemia patients, patients receiving double Cord Blood grafts, and those undergoing non-myeloablative HSCT.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Good clinical outcomes post-HSCT depend on proper immune reconstitution, with T cells being responsible for both GVL effect and infection protection. Profound immunodeficiency and risk of opportunistic infections characterize the first months post-HSCT. Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) causes significant morbidity and mortality, however, patients developing GVHD after HSCT showed a significantly lower risk of relapse. Discontinuation of immunosuppression with resulting GVHD can re-establish remission in relapsed leukemia. HSCT offers a survival advantage for patients with late-stage malignant disorders. TREC quantification is critical for early diagnosis and improved outcomes in SCID, and for understanding the pathophysiology of other immunodeficiencies. It monitors thymic activity and treatment efficacy in HIV infection. In autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis, it highlights impaired thymic function as a potential disease feature or contributor to pathogenesis. Post-HSCT, TREC predicts immune recovery, T cell reconstitution, and is used to predict the risk of infection (opportunistic, bacterial, CMV), relapse, overall survival, transplant-related mortality (TRM), and the risk of developing GVHD. Age is negatively correlated with TREC levels, accounting for poor prognosis in adults compared to young children after HSCT. Low or absent TREC levels are significantly correlated with severe infections and relapse. TREC measurement can evaluate the current status of reconstituting functional T cell immunity and has high predictive value for outcomes.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: TREC monitoring is a predictive marker for complications and clinical outcome (diagnostic utility/risk stratification). Profound immunodeficiency post-HSCT creates an adverse risk for opportunistic infections. GVHD is an adverse risk due to morbidity and mortality. T cell depletion can eliminate GVHD risk but significantly increases relapse risk (adverse risk). The GVL effect and GVHD occurrence correlating with lower relapse risk offer a protective benefit. Diagnostic Utility (SCID screening, immunodeficiency assessment); Predictive Utility (HIV treatment monitoring, immune recovery post-HSCT, risk of infection/relapse/mortality/GVHD); Adverse Risk (low TREC levels in HIV, RA, MS, severe infections, relapse, TRM, GVHD, poor prognosis in adults, delayed thymic function with acute GVHD); Protective Benefit (increased TREC after HIV treatment, high TREC levels linked to better survival, lower infection risk, improved OS/PFS, efficient T cell reconstitution, reduced TRM, faster immune reconstitution in pediatric patients with prolonged mixed chimerism).

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: Detection of TRECs by PCR is a reliable method for estimating newly formed T cells and thymic function. However, TREC measurements show 'great variation' due to methodological differences (absolute vs. relative quantification, different cell subpopulations, different units of expression) and a lack of randomized studies, variations in conditioning regimen protocols. Indirect methods like phenotyping na	ifve T cells and chest-computed tomography (CT) are considered 'not reliable' for evaluating thymic output. The SYBR-Green dye method is 'less specific' compared to the gold-standard real-time PCR based on TaqMan site-specific probes. SjTREC levels are influenced by factors such as longevity of na	ifve T cells, peripheral expansion, apoptosis, and intracellular degradation, requiring careful interpretation. TREC data are acknowledged to be hampered by several clinical and experimental factors and do not necessarily reflect a dynamic measurement of thymic output. However, TREC has proven to be the best non-invasive, feasible screening tool for SCID and is clinically implemented. A limitation of CD31 as an RTE marker is that not all CD31+ cells are necessarily RTE. The method of calculating TREC as a ratio between signal-joint TRECs (sjTREC) and a housekeeping gene in purified CD3+ cells appears to improve accuracy, especially when combined with data on ongoing cell proliferation to compensate for peripheral expansion. There is a need for consensus on TREC analysis methods to achieve comparable results across centers and for large multivariate and multicenter analyses to clarify dominant factors influencing TREC levels.
